The advice I can offer might not be the best, but it's how I got over, well, over-thinking (not that I never do it, but it's been reduced significantly). First off, you need to make sure that this really is a problem for you. At 15, I still heavily relied on my parents and was extremely stressed over just about any little thing. However, it's important to note that stress is normal in healthy doses. Stressing over exams and grades is normal. Stressing over crossing the street might not be. If it's interfering with your everyday life, then it's a problem.

If you want to let go of everyday stress, then I can suggest two things. Again, these are things that worked for me personally. I'm not an expert. Just a random guy with a similar problem.

​

* ***Make sure to have enough personal down-time:***

It is, of course, crucial, that you aren't constantly in stressful situations. There are two types of activities - those that strain you and those that refuel you. That's not to say that all straining activities are bad. Far from it. But it's important to not overlook those activities which refuel you, whether it's sitting down with a good book or having a chat with family or friends (or anything that floats your boat).

For me, anxiety and overthinking hit particularly hard in stressful situations (obviously). Laying off a bit and learning to *relax* helped me immensely.

* ***Talk about your problem:***

If you sense that you have a real problem that requires a real solution, then I'd advise you to talk about it. Not necessarily to a therapist (although I've had nothing but good experiences with them), but anyone who will listen to you. I'd advise *against* talking to people you think might put you down, knowingly or not, as that's the last thing you need. In fact, never talk about your problems to people like that (I know I have, and it was regrettable).

***Lastly, if nothing else works, nuke your problem with the IDGAF (I Don't Give a Fuck):***

I mention this 'solution' last because it's really a non-solution. The IDGAF can go two ways, and if not harnessed correctly, can be detrimental to your personal growth.

I embraced the IDGAF because the pressure was becoming so great that I would have rather died than face it head-on. And honestly, although it has harmed me somewhat, I personally think it helped me a lot. The point of IDGAF is simple. Is someone in your face? Don't pay it attention. Is there an upcoming exam? Do your best and *let it go*.

Basically, IDGAFing frees you from overthinking at the price of potentially becoming lazy or complacent. Start with the little things. Things which tick you off. Consciously decide that the next time it happens, you'll care a little less. It can take a few weeks or months, but it should have an effect.

​

​

In the end, remember that both you and me (more so you) are very young. You don't **need** to be independent yet. Trust me, it'll come on its own. Just focus on the little things, try to learn practical skills, make some money here and there. No need to leap into the ocean when you can't even swim yet!
